newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa grants amnesty as new requests pour in.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa grants amnesty as new requests pour in.

text.p: South Africa's post-apartheid "truth commission" on Thursday pardoned four anti-democracy white bombers and three anti-apartheid black vigilantes for human rights crimes in the final days of white rule.

Ruling on 16 applications, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) headed by Archbishop Desmond Tutu granted and refused applications by self-confessed perpetrators of human rights crimes on both sides of the struggle over apartheid.

The whites given amnesty were four right-wingers responsible for bombings shortly after Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) began democracy talks with then president F.W. de Klerk's white-led National Party.
The three blacks pardoned were members of an ANC-aligned self-defence unit that killed three black gangsters terrorising their township near Kroonstad.
"They walk as if the offence had never happened," Alex Boraine, deputy chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told a news conference.

He said nine people in prison for crimes including murder were denied amnesty, some because they had not served recognised political groups and others because they committed their crimes for personal and not for political reasons.
They included Kwane Sebe, son of former apartheid homeland leader Lennox Sebe, who is in jail for attacking the homes of people judged by the commission to be personal rivals.

Conservative Party leader Ferdi Hartzenberg, who refused to take part in the country's first democratic elections in 1994, attacked the decision against six Afrikaners, including four brothers who got drunk and killed two black security guards.
"This indicates again that the sole intention of the TRC is the destruction of the Afrikaner," he said.

The rulings were issued a day after white former policeman Brian Mitchell was pardoned for organising an attack in which 11 blacks died in 1988 and just days before the midnight Saturday deadline for amnesty applications.
Boraine said the commission would renew its request to Mandela on Friday to extend the deadline for applications by about three months.

He said the commission would also ask Mandela to broaden the scope of the commission's work to include right-wing bombings that killed at least 21 people in the final days before the first all-race elections in April 1994.

Mandela has so far resisted pressure from Tutu to extend the deadline and some ANC leaders have argued that veterans of the movement's guerrilla army do not need amnesty for actions that were part of "a just war".
The ANC said on Thursday that former guerrillas including Defence Minister Joe Modise and Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils would file amnesty applications on Friday.
"The enthusiasm demonstrated by all our members concerned is indicative of the commitment of our movement to help heal the nation of its wounds," the ANC said in a statement.
The party said about 300 of the almost 4,000 amnesty applications already filed were from ANC members, including veterans of its army, Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK, Spear of the Nation).
De Klerk, who has not sought amnesty, said in a statement on Wednesday he did not believe that former apartheid policemen and soldiers needed to seek amnesty for carrying out orders.
Boraine said the commission had prepared a list of questions for former president P.W. Botha, who has so far refused to testify to the commission or to seek amnesty.

"Our view is that anyone who was directly responsible and in charge of a system that brought about gross human rights violations in this country not only owes South Africa an apology, but ought, in the interests of reconciliation, to give very serious consideration to applying for amnesty," he said.
